57:   │              + full admission state machine (protection / backfill class /
58:   │              temporal credit / frontier distance)
59:   ├── Paged KV page accounting + block tables (device pages reported by the leaf)
60:   ├── KV-RAM host tier (probation / protected eviction) + prefix reuse *(in progress: G4)*

63:   └── crates/runtime: safe wrapper over the step ABI *(shipped: G1)*
64:         │
65: Step-level C ABI (device-resident, opaque handles — ADR 0009)
66:   model load · sequence alloc/release/snapshot · prefill(span, pos)
67:   · decode round(batch) · sampling params · stats
68:         │
69: Kernel leaf (kernel/, C++/CUDA static lib — CMake + nvcc, SM120a)
70:   ├── program: device arena, streams, the 64-layer op sequence,
71:   │            sequence state (KV pages, fp32 GDN slots, conv taps)

1: # The vendored reference subtree
2: 
3: Everything under `kernel/vendor/` except this file is a **verbatim copy** of a
4: file from the reference engine (ninfer) at one pinned commit. Nothing here is
5: written or edited by hand. That is the whole point of ADR 0010: a port claim
6: must be diffable, so "we ported the reference's kernel" means *this exact file
7: is the reference's file*, and a script proves it.
8: 
9: - Policy: `docs/adr/0010-vendored-reference-kernels.md`
10: - Attribution: `kernel/NOTICE` (the subtree is Apache-2.0; `LICENSE` is
11:   vendored alongside the code)
12: - Spec: `.scratch/runtime/specs/01-device-resident-forward.md` (GitHub #36)
13: 
14: ## The manifest
15: 
16: `kernel/vendor/manifest.json` is the source of truth for what is vendored.
17: 
18: ```json
19: {
20:   "reference": { "repo": "…", "branch": "…", "commit": "…", "default_path": "…" },
21:   "vendor_root": "kernel/vendor",
22:   "files": [
23:     { "path": "src/core/arena.h", "sha256": "…" },
24:     { "path": "src/core/arena.cu", "sha256": "…",
25:       "patch": { "diff": "patches/src/core/arena.cu.diff", "sha256": "…", "reason": "…" } }
26:   ]
27: }
28: ```
29: 
30: - `reference.commit` is the **only** revision the hashes describe. Vendoring
31:   from any other checkout state is a hash mismatch, not a merge.
32: - `path` is shared by the reference and the leaf: `src/core/arena.h` in the
33:   reference is `kernel/vendor/src/core/arena.h` here. Vendored files keep the
34:   reference's namespaces and include paths (`#include "core/arena.h"`,
35:   `#include "ops/common/math.cuh"`), so a `diff` against the source is trivial
36:   and a reference update is a re-run of the script — never a re-port.
37: - `sha256` is the file's content hash **in the reference**. A vendored file
38:   must be byte-identical to it unless the entry records a `patch`.
39: - `.gitattributes` marks the subtree `-text` so git never rewrites the line
40:   endings the hashes describe.
41: 
42: ## The script
43: 
44: `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1` wraps the `vendor-ninfer` binary of
45: `crates/vendor`. The logic lives in a Rust crate rather than in the script so
46: that `cargo test` covers it (`docs/agents/testing.md`).
47: 
48: | Command | What it does |
49: |---|---|
50: | `verify` | Every listed file exists under `kernel/vendor/` and hashes to what the manifest expects. With a reference checkout present, also checks the reference still carries the pinned content. **This is the byte-identical check.** |
51: | `sync` | Copies every listed file from the reference into the leaf. Verifies the reference against the pinned hashes *first* and copies nothing on a mismatch, so a wrong checkout cannot half-overwrite the subtree. Files with a recorded patch are kept unless `--force-patched`. |
52: | `repin` | Recomputes the hashes from the checkout on disk. Used when moving to a new reference commit — set `reference.commit` in the same change. |
53: | `record-patch PATH --reason TEXT` | Writes the local edit out as a diff under `patches/` and records its patched hash. |
54: 
55: Options: `--reference PATH` (defaults to `reference.default_path`, or
56: `$IGNIS_NINFER_REFERENCE`), `--manifest PATH`. Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` a
57: verification finding, `2` a usage or I/O error. `verify` works without a
58: reference checkout, so it runs from a bare clone.
59: 
60: ```powershell
61: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 verify
62: ```
63: 
64: ## The patch policy
65: 
66: A vendored file may not be edited. When the leaf genuinely needs a local
67: change, it is **recorded**, never silently applied:
68: 
69: 1. edit the file under `kernel/vendor/`;
70: 2. `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 record-patch <path> --reason "<why>"` — this
71:    writes `patches/<path>.diff` and sets the entry's `patch.sha256` to the
72:    patched content's hash;
73: 3. commit the diff with the file.
74: 
75: From then on `verify` expects the *patched* hash locally and the *reference's*
76: hash upstream, so both an unrecorded edit and upstream drift are caught. `sync`
77: will not overwrite a patched file unless it is told to.
78: 
79: Anything that is not a verbatim vendored file — including a file we edit
80: beyond a recorded patch — is our own implementation and carries no provenance
81: claim (ADR 0010). The leaf's own code lives in `kernel/src/`,
82: `kernel/include/` and `kernel/tests/`, never here.

474:   `ops/launcher/prepare_masked_block.{h,cu}`,
475:   `ops/wrapper/prepare_masked_block.cpp`, `ninfer/ops/prepare_masked_block.h`:

477: - **cast** — `ops/kernel/cast.cuh`, `ops/launcher/cast.{h,cu}`,
478:   `ops/wrapper/cast.cpp`, `ninfer/ops/cast.h`: the exact BF16 → FP32 widening
479:   the selector scores take.

481:   `test_prepare_masked_block.cpp` and `test_cast.cpp`, unmodified, in the
482:   `ignis_<op>_test` CTest loop.
483: - Not vendored: `prepare_ragged_prefix` and `scatter`, which the reference uses
484:   to carry the verified columns' taps into the *next* round. ignis appends
485:   them to the window at the end of the same round instead
486:   (`kernel/src/dflash2_drafter.cu`, ours), so no tap outlives its round.

488: GitHub #177 (Vision 3/7) vendors the ops the vision tower runs on, at the same
489: pinned commit:
490: 
491: - **vision encoder ops** — `layer_norm`, `gelu` (tanh and exact modes),
492:   `add_bias`, `vision_pos_embed` (the bilinear 48×48 position-table add) and
493:   `vision_attention` (segmented, `cu_seqlens` per image): each op's kernel
494:   (`src/ops/kernel`), launcher (`src/ops/launcher`), wrapper
495:   (`src/ops/wrapper`) and public header (`include/ninfer/ops`).
496: - **scatter** — the same four files: it writes the encoder's `[5120, V]`
497:   output over a prefill span's placeholder columns.
498: - **prepare_ragged_prefix** — the same four files, vendored because the
499:   reference's `test_scatter.cpp` calls it; nothing in the leaf does.
500: - **Q4/Q5/Q6 row-split linear** — `src/ops/linear/q4/`, `q5/` and `q6/` in
501:   full (dispatch, GEMV, small-T / SIMT / MMA kernels, and the q6 storage
502:   header; the q4/q5 storage headers were already vendored). The leaf's own

505: - Vision RoPE frequencies need nothing new: `rope_vision_frequencies` and the
506:   Vision rotation mode live in the already-vendored `rope` family (P1-15).
507: - **their reference tests** — `tests/ops/test_{layer_norm,gelu,add_bias,
508:   vision_pos_embed,vision_attention,scatter}.cpp`, unmodified, in the
509:   `ignis_<op>_test` CTest loop; `tests/ops/linear/test_{q4,q5,q6}_a16.cpp`,

Why this fork
The upstream engine wasn't built with coding-agent workloads in mind. A tool like Qwen Code fires
bursts of near-identical subagent requests that share the same long system prompt and tool schemas
(often 98% identical) and diverge only in a short task-specific tail — but the engine had a single
global prefill lane with no concept of "these requests are mostly the same": every subagent redid
the full prefill from scratch, serialized one behind another, producing time-to-first-token ladders
of several seconds per subagent even though almost none of that work was actually new. A
long-running main conversation and a one-shot classifier call were also indistinguishable to the
scheduler, so the conversation the user was waiting on could get evicted and re-prefilled at the
worst possible moment. This fork exists to fix that: optimize the engine specifically for
coding-tool usage patterns.
What's added in this fork

Host-RAM KV cache tier (two-tier probation/protected eviction) that snapshots finished or
still-decoding GPU lanes so a sibling request can restore instead of re-prefilling
Prefix-reuse and admission logic so concurrent identical or shared-prefix requests (a subagent
burst sharing one long system+tools prompt) skip the redundant part of prefill entirely
Tagged request lanes (@main/@agents/@classifier, see below) so the scheduler knows which
lane is the long-lived conversation and protects it from eviction by short-lived traffic
DFlash2 speculative decoding made to actually run end-to-end on this tree (gather/selector
addressing bugs fixed, RAM-tier KV carry for the drafter, working presets)
Two silent KV-corruption bugs found and fixed (a rewrite-checkpoint restore and a hyperquant
exact-key side store, both serving one request with another's state)
Streaming/tool-call-parsing hardening, adaptive MTP verification-width calibration from measured
round cost

Measured effect: siblings that used to pay a full prefill (hundreds to thousands of ms) now restore
in tens to a few hundred ms, and a burst of subagents sharing a system+tools prefix reuses ~99% of
it instead of queueing behind each other's redundant prefill.

Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.8-27B each expose two registered weight profiles. The version-2 artifact
identity selects the profile without a separate runtime flag; Qwen3.8 uses target key
qwen3_8_27b while sharing the 27B execution package. The Qwen3.6 nvfp4 profile uses W4A4 Tensor
Core MMA for prefill and A16 NVFP4 kernels for decode. The Qwen3.8 nvfp4 profile preserves its
source's mixed allocation: NVFP4 MLP weights in Text layers 0–55 and row-scaled FP8 for the token
embedding, attention input/output projections, GDN Q/K/V/Z and output projections, output head, and
remaining MLP weights. All four 27B artifacts retain the same Text, Vision, MTP, prefix-reuse, CLI,
and serving routes.
Upstream lineage
NInfer is Neroued's project
(Neroued/ninfer); that repository remains the reference
implementation, and master here follows upstream/master directly. This workspace builds on
natpate/ninfer-windows, the native Windows port of
that engine — the port core below is inherited from it (the compatibility layer itself ported
from Don-Chad/ninfer-3090, without its RTX 3090
retargeting). The WebUI and context-reporting items live on this fork's feat/windows-port
lineage — natpate's dev branch has already absorbed them, and PR #2
delivers them to its master.
Windows-port lineage:

Native Windows 11 x64 build and run — CMake with Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC), with
vcpkg resolving FFmpeg, libcurl, and zlib via the
vcpkg.json manifest; the CUDA runtime is statically linked, so the CUDA Toolkit is only
needed at build time.
Windows porting of the runtime — memory-mapped artifact reading with unbuffered
overlapped I/O (the Windows counterpart of POSIX O_DIRECT/pread, with the same 4096-byte
alignment contract), portable console logging and load progress, and portable media
acquisition for image and video input.
MSVC/TMA kernel compatibility — fixes that let the upstream Blackwell kernels compile
under MSVC: device-pointer NVFP4 TMA descriptors, the pair-row SwiGLU TMA epilogue, and
MSVC move-construction details in the target runtime.
Stock llama.cpp WebUI — the HTTP server additionally accepts the stock llama.cpp WebUI's
API dialect, and ninfer-serve can serve the unmodified WebUI in-process: --webui
downloads the latest build from the
ggml-org/llama-ui bucket on first start, or
--webui-dir DIR serves an existing local copy.
Context window reporting — ninfer-serve advertises the served context ceiling in the
OpenAI dialect: the objects returned by /v1/models and /v1/models/{id} carry
meta.n_ctx = the --max-context value in force.
Portable Windows release — a self-contained zip containing the executables and all
runtime DLLs; see Prebuilt Windows release.

What this fork adds on top (one squashed commit per feature branch, per
About this fork):

feat/qwen3.8-nvfp4full — the Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 full-precision-requant artifact:
unified activation scale space, conversion tooling, model card, and the published gpqa
comparison.
feat/hyperquant — the hq-e8-2b KV cache: E8-lattice + Rice entropy coding at
2.25 bits/scalar (3.7× smaller payload than INT8 at 262k context), prompt attention over
one-shot decoded rotated bf16 scratch, an 8-lane cooperative k=0 Rice decoder with a
parallel unary packer, and a tensor-core tile-source decode kernel (the hq route is a
KV-source policy of the bf16 TC kernel). After the residual-window + dither work below,
hq decode matches or beats same-session INT8 at the measured cells (tg128 80.6 vs 71.7,
pp32k+tg64 62.2 vs 58.1 tok/s).
feat/1m-context — the 1M-context track: engine envelope raised to 1,048,576 keys on
the U8 cache (banded rotated scratch, 1M + --kv-capacity auto resolves the full pool with
~3.3 GiB free), YaRN rope scaling (--rope-scaling yarn:F[,t=][,bf=][,bs=], q-side
temperature, FP64 angle reduction), the bf16/int8 linear envelope raised to 524,288 keys,
and the WI-8 quality fix — a BF16 sink+recent residual window (S=32/W=512 exact side rows
with per-slot ring validity) plus half-cell subtractive dither, which fixed the >262k hq
garble: greedy needle retrieval is exact at 32k/304k/390k/592k true tokens (592k runs
yarn:4 at 916–922 prefill / 15.2 decode tok/s; MTP3 at 390k commits 62.9 tok/s). Beyond
~592k the 1M cell still garbles (depth-independent; dense-YaRN-at-1M is the leading
suspect — see HANDOFF).

Everything else — the Linux build path, the RTX 5090 (sm_120a) target, the CUDA 13.1
requirement, and the NVFP4/W4A4 Blackwell execution paths — is unchanged from upstream.

Requirements
NInfer currently requires:

64-bit Linux or Windows 11 x64;
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120a);
NVIDIA driver support for CUDA 13.1 and the CUDA Toolkit 13.1 or newer;
CMake 3.28 or newer and a C++20-capable host compiler (GCC or Clang on Linux, MSVC from
Visual Studio 2022 on Windows);
FFmpeg development libraries: libavformat >= 60, libavcodec >= 60,
libavutil >= 58, and libswscale >= 7;
libcurl >= 7.85;
pkg-config on Linux, or vcpkg on Windows (the
repository pins the dependency baseline in vcpkg.json);
Ninja, when using the commands below.

The build rejects CUDA architectures other than 120a. On Linux, NInfer is run from its
source build tree; on Windows, the prebuilt portable release
provides the same binaries without a toolchain.
Prebuilt Windows release
Windows users who would rather not build can use the portable release instead of the build
steps below. The zip is self-contained — executables, all runtime DLLs (FFmpeg,
libcurl, zlib, and the VC++ runtime; the CUDA runtime is statically linked), launcher scripts,
a models\ folder, a README.txt, and SHA256SUMS:

Download the latest ninfer-windows-<version>-win64-cuda131.zip from
GitHub Releases. Verify files against
SHA256SUMS, e.g. Get-FileHash ninfer-serve.exe -Algorithm SHA256.
Extract it anywhere — the launcher scripts use relative paths and work from any location.
Download a model into models\ as in Download a model.
Run the matching launcher, e.g. .\qwen3_8_27b.bat. This starts ninfer-serve on
http://127.0.0.1:8080 (API at /v1) and serves the WebUI at the root URL; --webui
downloads the WebUI on first start, so the first run needs an internet connection (later
runs reuse the local copy).
Or run .\ninfer-serve.exe models\<model>.ninfer [flags] directly — the options are
identical to a source build (see Run the HTTP server).

The launchers default to a 150,000-token context (--max-context / --default-max-tokens) to
leave VRAM headroom for the Windows desktop. On the 32 GB RTX 5090, the smaller models
(qwen3_6_27b, qwen3_6_27b_nvfp4, and qwen3_8_27b) can be safely raised to 200,000 when
VRAM is completely free at startup; the two larger models (qwen3_8_27b_nvfp4 and
qwen3_6_35b_a3b) do not fit at 200,000 and should stay at 150,000. Hardware requirements are
unchanged: Windows 11 x64, RTX 5090, and an NVIDIA driver supporting CUDA 13.1.
Build
Linux
git clone https://github.com/cometkim/ninfer.git
cd ninfer

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel
The default configuration builds:
build/apps/ninfer
build/apps/ninfer-serve

Tests, benchmarks, and maintainer tools are excluded from the default build.
Windows
The fork's build entry point is a pair of plain-PowerShell Ninja wrappers — no developer
prompt needed. configure-ninja.ps1 (run once per build directory) imports the MSVC
(vcvars64) environment itself, resolves cmake/ninja from PATH with VS-bundled and
winget fallbacks, points the vcpkg toolchain at VCPKG_ROOT (falling back to this
machine's local checkout) and nvcc at CUDA_PATH, and enables tests and benchmarks by
default (-NoTests / -NoBenchmarks exclude them). build-ninja.ps1 builds everything
or one target:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File configure-ninja.ps1
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File build-ninja.ps1
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File build-ninja.ps1 -Target ninfer_bench

build-ninja/apps/ninfer.exe
build-ninja/apps/ninfer-serve.exe

launcher TUs are split per dtype (and per geometry for the hq codec kernels), so a cold
build takes ~15 minutes on the RTX 5090 box versus ~50 minutes through the Visual Studio
generator, and touching a launcher dispatcher rebuilds in ~90 seconds. MSVC compiles with
/utf-8 for source and execution charset, matching the Linux toolchain default.

  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \

HTTP serving.
Request lanes for coding agents (@main / @agents / @classifier)
(gpillon fork addition — see About this fork above for why this exists.)
Append @main, @agents, or @classifier to the model field to tell the scheduler what kind of
request this is, so lane eviction and prefix reuse can treat it accordingly:



Tag
For
Eviction priority




@main
the long-lived, user-facing conversation
protected — ranked last among eviction candidates, so short-lived traffic never forces it to re-prefill


@agents
short-lived subagent/tool-delegation calls (also the default for an untagged model id)
recycled freely


@classifier
one-shot intent/routing/classification calls
recycled freely



# The user-facing conversation — protect this lane from eviction.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.6-27b@main",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Continue the conversation."}],
    "max_tokens": 512
  }'

# A subagent spawned by the main conversation — freely recyclable, and if its
# prompt shares a long system+tools prefix with a sibling already running
# (the common case for a burst of subagents from the same tool), it reuses
# that prefix instead of re-prefilling.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.6-27b@agents",
    "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "<same long system+tools prompt>"},
                 {"role": "user", "content": "<subagent task N>"}],
    "max_tokens": 256
  }'

# A one-shot intent classifier — same recycling tier as @agents, kept
# separate so its churn is visible on its own in the throughput log.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.6-27b@classifier",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Classify: <text>"}],
    "max_tokens": 8
  }'
Benefits in practice: fire ten subagent requests against @agents while a @main conversation is
mid-decode, and the main conversation's lane is never chosen as the eviction victim — the subagents
recycle each other's lanes first. Subagents sharing a system+tools prefix restore most of it from
the host-RAM cache instead of re-prefilling, so time-to-first-token drops from full-prefill latency
(hundreds of ms to multiple seconds, depending on prompt length) to the cost of re-hashing and
copying a cached prefix (tens to a couple hundred ms). Untagged requests keep working exactly as
before, classified as @agents.
Capabilities
All three registered model IDs support:

text generation with thinking and non-thinking prompt modes;
image, multi-image, video, and mixed multimodal messages;
chunked prefill and CUDA Graph decode;
startup-bounded small-scale concurrent serving with true batched decode;
fixed or signal-adaptive MTP speculative decoding with draft windows from one to eight on 27B
targets and one to five on 35B-A3B;
BF16 and INT8 group-64 KV cache;
model- and thinking-mode-aware official sampling defaults, with explicit greedy, temperature,
top-k, top-p, min-p, and presence/frequency-penalty overrides;
compatible-prefix reuse;
OpenAI Responses Core, OpenAI Chat Completions, and Anthropic Messages, including streaming and
usage accounting;
prompt-rendered function tools and parsed tool calls.

The 35B-A3B target additionally supports text-only DFlash speculative decoding with draft windows
from one to fifteen.
Current limits

Only the five (model_id, weights_id) artifact identities listed above are accepted product
identities.
Execution is specialized for one RTX 5090 and one CUDA device.
One Engine owns one resident model and supports a startup-fixed capacity of 1–8 active requests.
Decode-ready requests are compacted at round boundaries and executed in one batched model
traversal.
NInfer does not provide large-scale or preemptive continuous batching, priority/QoS scheduling,
multi-GPU execution, CPU/GPU offload, or distributed serving.
--max-context is the logical ceiling of each sequence and is configurable up to the registered
models' per-dtype context envelope: 524,288 tokens with bf16/int8 KV and 1,048,576
with hq-e8-2b (YaRN --rope-scaling yarn:F past the checkpoint's trained 262,144
positions). --kv-capacity N explicitly sizes the shared Main Text KV
pool for all active and retained sequences, while --kv-capacity auto selects the largest usable
capacity from the memory remaining after weights are loaded while preserving 1 GiB of sizing
headroom. Omission defaults to one --max-context worth of pages. The resolved pool is fixed at
startup and is not divided statically among request lanes.
Tool calls are parsed and returned to the client; NInfer does not execute tools.
The C++ headers are used by the in-tree applications and are not distributed as an installed SDK.

# Git and GitHub
- Only commit, amend, push, or create PRs when explicitly requested.
- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.
- Write a concise commit message that matches the repo style.
- Do not update git config, skip hooks, use interactive `-i`, force-push, or create empty commits unless explicitly requested.
- If a commit fails or hooks reject it, fix the issue and create a new commit; do not amend the failed commit.
- Before creating a PR, inspect status, diff, remote tracking, recent commits, and the diff from the base branch.
- Review all commits included in the PR, not just the latest commit.
- Use `gh` for GitHub tasks, including PRs, issues, checks, and releases; return the PR URL when done.

Issues live **exclusively on GitHub** (`gpillon/ignis`, via the `gh` CLI).

1: # ignis
2: 
3: A high-throughput inference engine for **Qwen 3.8-27B** on a single **NVIDIA
4: RTX 5090** (SM120a), serving an **OpenAI-compatible HTTP API** from a Rust core
5: backed by a C++/CUDA kernel leaf.
6: 
7: **Status:** early development — **the engine now serves real completions on
8: the GPU.** With `IGNIS_ARTIFACT` set and the binary built with `--features
9: cuda`, `ignis-server` loads the model onto the device and drives the real
10: 64-layer program (device-resident, step-level C ABI — ADR 0009, verbatim-
11: vendored reference kernels — ADR 0010) for both streaming and non-streaming
12: chat completions, stopping on the model's own EOS token or `max_tokens`.
13: Without an artifact, or without `--features cuda`, it falls back to the
14: deterministic CPU-only mock (`MockCompute`, ADR 0006) for protocol and loop
15: work.
16: 
17: **Gate history:** G1 GREEN (2026-09-07, 97.1% teacher-forced canary
18: agreement), G2 GREEN (2026-09-09, TTFT ratios 0.878/0.851 on the 8K/32K
19: cells), G3 closed 2026-09-10 with one open gap (#110, the ITL p95 cell).
20: **Next milestone: the G4 gate run** (master #65, the reference feature
21: floor) — hq-e8-2b KV as a load option, snapshot/restore + KV-RAM host tier,
22: device prefix reuse, unified eviction, tagged lanes; verdict is the 99%

24: The full phase/gate plan is `.scratch/ROADMAP.md`; the review that reset it

29: ## What it is
30: 
31: `ignis` is a deliberately specialized inference engine: one model family, one
32: GPU class. It is **not** a recreation of the reference stack (NInfer) — it is a
33: new architecture that borrows proven kernel work where it helps.
34: 
35: - **Performance-first.** Correctness (a self-check of *sane* output) is a
36:   non-negotiable floor; above it, performance is the #1 objective. The
37:   north-star is *"the best local coding engine"* — maximum throughput **and**
38:   agent parallelism that saturates the GPU in prefill *and* decode.
39: - **Rust core + C++/CUDA leaf.** Rust owns everything above the *step* —
40:   scheduling, KV accounting, serving; the forward pass and all GPU compute live
41:   in a static C++/CUDA library behind a flat, device-resident step-level C ABI
42:   (ADR 0009).
43: 
44: The engine is also its own dogfood target: good enough to run a developer's own
45: concurrent coding agent (a "1 main agent + N subagents" load).

58:   │              temporal credit / frontier distance)
59:   ├── Paged KV page accounting + block tables (device pages reported by the leaf)
60:   ├── KV-RAM host tier (probation / protected eviction) + prefix reuse *(in progress: G4)*

67:   · decode round(batch) · sampling params · stats
68:         │
69: Kernel leaf (kernel/, C++/CUDA static lib — CMake + nvcc, SM120a)
70:   ├── program: device arena, streams, the 64-layer op sequence,

1: # The vendored reference subtree
2: 
3: Everything under `kernel/vendor/` except this file is a **verbatim copy** of a
4: file from the reference engine (ninfer) at one pinned commit. Nothing here is
5: written or edited by hand. That is the whole point of ADR 0010: a port claim
6: must be diffable, so "we ported the reference's kernel" means *this exact file
7: is the reference's file*, and a script proves it.
8: 
9: - Policy: `docs/adr/0010-vendored-reference-kernels.md`
10: - Attribution: `kernel/NOTICE` (the subtree is Apache-2.0; `LICENSE` is
11:   vendored alongside the code)
12: - Spec: `.scratch/runtime/specs/01-device-resident-forward.md` (GitHub #36)
13: 
14: ## The manifest
15: 
16: `kernel/vendor/manifest.json` is the source of truth for what is vendored.
17: 
18: ```json
19: {
20:   "reference": { "repo": "…", "branch": "…", "commit": "…", "default_path": "…" },
21:   "vendor_root": "kernel/vendor",
22:   "files": [
23:     { "path": "src/core/arena.h", "sha256": "…" },
24:     { "path": "src/core/arena.cu", "sha256": "…",
25:       "patch": { "diff": "patches/src/core/arena.cu.diff", "sha256": "…", "reason": "…" } }
26:   ]
27: }
28: ```
29: 
30: - `reference.commit` is the **only** revision the hashes describe. Vendoring
31:   from any other checkout state is a hash mismatch, not a merge.
32: - `path` is shared by the reference and the leaf: `src/core/arena.h` in the
33:   reference is `kernel/vendor/src/core/arena.h` here. Vendored files keep the
34:   reference's namespaces and include paths (`#include "core/arena.h"`,
35:   `#include "ops/common/math.cuh"`), so a `diff` against the source is trivial
36:   and a reference update is a re-run of the script — never a re-port.
37: - `sha256` is the file's content hash **in the reference**. A vendored file
38:   must be byte-identical to it unless the entry records a `patch`.
39: - `.gitattributes` marks the subtree `-text` so git never rewrites the line
40:   endings the hashes describe.
41: 
42: ## The script
43: 
44: `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1` wraps the `vendor-ninfer` binary of
45: `crates/vendor`. The logic lives in a Rust crate rather than in the script so
46: that `cargo test` covers it (`docs/agents/testing.md`).
47: 
48: | Command | What it does |
49: |---|---|
50: | `verify` | Every listed file exists under `kernel/vendor/` and hashes to what the manifest expects. With a reference checkout present, also checks the reference still carries the pinned content. **This is the byte-identical check.** |
51: | `sync` | Copies every listed file from the reference into the leaf. Verifies the reference against the pinned hashes *first* and copies nothing on a mismatch, so a wrong checkout cannot half-overwrite the subtree. Files with a recorded patch are kept unless `--force-patched`. |
52: | `repin` | Recomputes the hashes from the checkout on disk. Used when moving to a new reference commit — set `reference.commit` in the same change. |
53: | `record-patch PATH --reason TEXT` | Writes the local edit out as a diff under `patches/` and records its patched hash. |
54: 
55: Options: `--reference PATH` (defaults to `reference.default_path`, or
56: `$IGNIS_NINFER_REFERENCE`), `--manifest PATH`. Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` a
57: verification finding, `2` a usage or I/O error. `verify` works without a
58: reference checkout, so it runs from a bare clone.
59: 
60: ```powershell
61: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 verify
62: ```
63: 
64: ## The patch policy
65: 
66: A vendored file may not be edited. When the leaf genuinely needs a local
67: change, it is **recorded**, never silently applied:
68: 
69: 1. edit the file under `kernel/vendor/`;
70: 2. `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 record-patch <path> --reason "<why>"` — this
71:    writes `patches/<path>.diff` and sets the entry's `patch.sha256` to the
72:    patched content's hash;
73: 3. commit the diff with the file.
74: 
75: From then on `verify` expects the *patched* hash locally and the *reference's*
76: hash upstream, so both an unrecorded edit and upstream drift are caught. `sync`
77: will not overwrite a patched file unless it is told to.
78: 
79: Anything that is not a verbatim vendored file — including a file we edit
80: beyond a recorded patch — is our own implementation and carries no provenance
81: claim (ADR 0010). The leaf's own code lives in `kernel/src/`,
82: `kernel/include/` and `kernel/tests/`, never here.

Why this fork
The upstream engine wasn't built with coding-agent workloads in mind. A tool like Qwen Code fires
bursts of near-identical subagent requests that share the same long system prompt and tool schemas
(often 98% identical) and diverge only in a short task-specific tail — but the engine had a single
global prefill lane with no concept of "these requests are mostly the same": every subagent redid
the full prefill from scratch, serialized one behind another, producing time-to-first-token ladders
of several seconds per subagent even though almost none of that work was actually new. A
long-running main conversation and a one-shot classifier call were also indistinguishable to the
scheduler, so the conversation the user was waiting on could get evicted and re-prefilled at the
worst possible moment. This fork exists to fix that: optimize the engine specifically for
coding-tool usage patterns.
What's added in this fork

Host-RAM KV cache tier (two-tier probation/protected eviction) that snapshots finished or
still-decoding GPU lanes so a sibling request can restore instead of re-prefilling
Prefix-reuse and admission logic so concurrent identical or shared-prefix requests (a subagent
burst sharing one long system+tools prompt) skip the redundant part of prefill entirely
Tagged request lanes (@main/@agents/@classifier, see below) so the scheduler knows which
lane is the long-lived conversation and protects it from eviction by short-lived traffic
DFlash2 speculative decoding made to actually run end-to-end on this tree (gather/selector
addressing bugs fixed, RAM-tier KV carry for the drafter, working presets)
Two silent KV-corruption bugs found and fixed (a rewrite-checkpoint restore and a hyperquant
exact-key side store, both serving one request with another's state)
Streaming/tool-call-parsing hardening, adaptive MTP verification-width calibration from measured
round cost

Measured effect: siblings that used to pay a full prefill (hundreds to thousands of ms) now restore
in tens to a few hundred ms, and a burst of subagents sharing a system+tools prefix reuses ~99% of
it instead of queueing behind each other's redundant prefill.

Selected checkpoints. Maximum single-GPU inference performance.

This fork carries Neroued/ninfer, a from-scratch C++/CUDA
inference engine for explicitly registered Qwen checkpoints on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090,

APIs, or the included llama.cpp webui. Development and measurement happen on Windows 11 x64
today (native builds via the port lineage); the Linux build path is unchanged from upstream and
is the intended next home for this environment.

Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.8-27B each expose two registered weight profiles. The version-2 artifact
identity selects the profile without a separate runtime flag; Qwen3.8 uses target key
qwen3_8_27b while sharing the 27B execution package. The Qwen3.6 nvfp4 profile uses W4A4 Tensor
Core MMA for prefill and A16 NVFP4 kernels for decode. The Qwen3.8 nvfp4 profile preserves its
source's mixed allocation: NVFP4 MLP weights in Text layers 0–55 and row-scaled FP8 for the token
embedding, attention input/output projections, GDN Q/K/V/Z and output projections, output head, and
remaining MLP weights. All four 27B artifacts retain the same Text, Vision, MTP, prefix-reuse, CLI,
and serving routes.
Upstream lineage
NInfer is Neroued's project
(Neroued/ninfer); that repository remains the reference
implementation, and master here follows upstream/master directly. This workspace builds on
natpate/ninfer-windows, the native Windows port of
that engine — the port core below is inherited from it (the compatibility layer itself ported
from Don-Chad/ninfer-3090, without its RTX 3090
retargeting). The WebUI and context-reporting items live on this fork's feat/windows-port
lineage — natpate's dev branch has already absorbed them, and PR #2
delivers them to its master.
Windows-port lineage:

Native Windows 11 x64 build and run — CMake with Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC), with
vcpkg resolving FFmpeg, libcurl, and zlib via the
vcpkg.json manifest; the CUDA runtime is statically linked, so the CUDA Toolkit is only
needed at build time.
Windows porting of the runtime — memory-mapped artifact reading with unbuffered
overlapped I/O (the Windows counterpart of POSIX O_DIRECT/pread, with the same 4096-byte
alignment contract), portable console logging and load progress, and portable media
acquisition for image and video input.
MSVC/TMA kernel compatibility — fixes that let the upstream Blackwell kernels compile
under MSVC: device-pointer NVFP4 TMA descriptors, the pair-row SwiGLU TMA epilogue, and
MSVC move-construction details in the target runtime.
Stock llama.cpp WebUI — the HTTP server additionally accepts the stock llama.cpp WebUI's
API dialect, and ninfer-serve can serve the unmodified WebUI in-process: --webui
downloads the latest build from the
ggml-org/llama-ui bucket on first start, or
--webui-dir DIR serves an existing local copy.
Context window reporting — ninfer-serve advertises the served context ceiling in the
OpenAI dialect: the objects returned by /v1/models and /v1/models/{id} carry
meta.n_ctx = the --max-context value in force.
Portable Windows release — a self-contained zip containing the executables and all
runtime DLLs; see Prebuilt Windows release.

What this fork adds on top (one squashed commit per feature branch, per
About this fork):

feat/qwen3.8-nvfp4full — the Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 full-precision-requant artifact:
unified activation scale space, conversion tooling, model card, and the published gpqa
comparison.
feat/hyperquant — the hq-e8-2b KV cache: E8-lattice + Rice entropy coding at
2.25 bits/scalar (3.7× smaller payload than INT8 at 262k context), prompt attention over
one-shot decoded rotated bf16 scratch, an 8-lane cooperative k=0 Rice decoder with a
parallel unary packer, and a tensor-core tile-source decode kernel (the hq route is a
KV-source policy of the bf16 TC kernel). After the residual-window + dither work below,
hq decode matches or beats same-session INT8 at the measured cells (tg128 80.6 vs 71.7,
pp32k+tg64 62.2 vs 58.1 tok/s).
feat/1m-context — the 1M-context track: engine envelope raised to 1,048,576 keys on
the U8 cache (banded rotated scratch, 1M + --kv-capacity auto resolves the full pool with
~3.3 GiB free), YaRN rope scaling (--rope-scaling yarn:F[,t=][,bf=][,bs=], q-side
temperature, FP64 angle reduction), the bf16/int8 linear envelope raised to 524,288 keys,
and the WI-8 quality fix — a BF16 sink+recent residual window (S=32/W=512 exact side rows
with per-slot ring validity) plus half-cell subtractive dither, which fixed the >262k hq
garble: greedy needle retrieval is exact at 32k/304k/390k/592k true tokens (592k runs
yarn:4 at 916–922 prefill / 15.2 decode tok/s; MTP3 at 390k commits 62.9 tok/s). Beyond
~592k the 1M cell still garbles (depth-independent; dense-YaRN-at-1M is the leading
suspect — see HANDOFF).

Everything else — the Linux build path, the RTX 5090 (sm_120a) target, the CUDA 13.1
requirement, and the NVFP4/W4A4 Blackwell execution paths — is unchanged from upstream.

Prebuilt Windows release
Windows users who would rather not build can use the portable release instead of the build
steps below. The zip is self-contained — executables, all runtime DLLs (FFmpeg,
libcurl, zlib, and the VC++ runtime; the CUDA runtime is statically linked), launcher scripts,
a models\ folder, a README.txt, and SHA256SUMS:

GitHub Releases. Verify files against
SHA256SUMS, e.g. Get-FileHash ninfer-serve.exe -Algorithm SHA256.
Extract it anywhere — the launcher scripts use relative paths and work from any location.
Download a model into models\ as in Download a model.
Run the matching launcher, e.g. .\qwen3_8_27b.bat. This starts ninfer-serve on
http://127.0.0.1:8080 (API at /v1) and serves the WebUI at the root URL; --webui

runs reuse the local copy).

identical to a source build (see Run the HTTP server).

leave VRAM headroom for the Windows desktop. On the 32 GB RTX 5090, the smaller models
(qwen3_6_27b, qwen3_6_27b_nvfp4, and qwen3_8_27b) can be safely raised to 200,000 when
VRAM is completely free at startup; the two larger models (qwen3_8_27b_nvfp4 and
qwen3_6_35b_a3b) do not fit at 200,000 and should stay at 150,000. Hardware requirements are

git clone https://github.com/cometkim/ninfer.git
cd ninfer

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

build/apps/ninfer
build/apps/ninfer-serve

Tests, benchmarks, and maintainer tools are excluded from the default build.
Windows
The fork's build entry point is a pair of plain-PowerShell Ninja wrappers — no developer

default (-NoTests / -NoBenchmarks exclude them). build-ninja.ps1 builds everything

build-ninja/apps/ninfer.exe
build-ninja/apps/ninfer-serve.exe

Request lanes for coding agents (@main / @agents / @classifier)
(gpillon fork addition — see About this fork above for why this exists.)
Append @main, @agents, or @classifier to the model field to tell the scheduler what kind of
request this is, so lane eviction and prefix reuse can treat it accordingly:



Tag
For
Eviction priority




@main
the long-lived, user-facing conversation
protected — ranked last among eviction candidates, so short-lived traffic never forces it to re-prefill


@agents
short-lived subagent/tool-delegation calls (also the default for an untagged model id)
recycled freely


@classifier
one-shot intent/routing/classification calls
recycled freely



# The user-facing conversation — protect this lane from eviction.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.6-27b@main",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Continue the conversation."}],
    "max_tokens": 512
  }'

# A subagent spawned by the main conversation — freely recyclable, and if its
# prompt shares a long system+tools prefix with a sibling already running
# (the common case for a burst of subagents from the same tool), it reuses
# that prefix instead of re-prefilling.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.6-27b@agents",
    "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "<same long system+tools prompt>"},
                 {"role": "user", "content": "<subagent task N>"}],
    "max_tokens": 256
  }'

# A one-shot intent classifier — same recycling tier as @agents, kept
# separate so its churn is visible on its own in the throughput log.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.6-27b@classifier",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Classify: <text>"}],
    "max_tokens": 8
  }'
Benefits in practice: fire ten subagent requests against @agents while a @main conversation is
mid-decode, and the main conversation's lane is never chosen as the eviction victim — the subagents
recycle each other's lanes first. Subagents sharing a system+tools prefix restore most of it from
the host-RAM cache instead of re-prefilling, so time-to-first-token drops from full-prefill latency
(hundreds of ms to multiple seconds, depending on prompt length) to the cost of re-hashing and
copying a cached prefix (tens to a couple hundred ms). Untagged requests keep working exactly as
before, classified as @agents.
Capabilities
All three registered model IDs support:

text generation with thinking and non-thinking prompt modes;
image, multi-image, video, and mixed multimodal messages;
chunked prefill and CUDA Graph decode;
startup-bounded small-scale concurrent serving with true batched decode;
fixed or signal-adaptive MTP speculative decoding with draft windows from one to eight on 27B
targets and one to five on 35B-A3B;
BF16 and INT8 group-64 KV cache;
model- and thinking-mode-aware official sampling defaults, with explicit greedy, temperature,
top-k, top-p, min-p, and presence/frequency-penalty overrides;
compatible-prefix reuse;
OpenAI Responses Core, OpenAI Chat Completions, and Anthropic Messages, including streaming and
usage accounting;
prompt-rendered function tools and parsed tool calls.

The 35B-A3B target additionally supports text-only DFlash speculative decoding with draft windows
from one to fifteen.
Current limits

Only the five (model_id, weights_id) artifact identities listed above are accepted product
identities.
Execution is specialized for one RTX 5090 and one CUDA device.
One Engine owns one resident model and supports a startup-fixed capacity of 1–8 active requests.
Decode-ready requests are compacted at round boundaries and executed in one batched model
traversal.
NInfer does not provide large-scale or preemptive continuous batching, priority/QoS scheduling,
multi-GPU execution, CPU/GPU offload, or distributed serving.
--max-context is the logical ceiling of each sequence and is configurable up to the registered
models' per-dtype context envelope: 524,288 tokens with bf16/int8 KV and 1,048,576
with hq-e8-2b (YaRN --rope-scaling yarn:F past the checkpoint's trained 262,144
positions). --kv-capacity N explicitly sizes the shared Main Text KV
pool for all active and retained sequences, while --kv-capacity auto selects the largest usable
capacity from the memory remaining after weights are loaded while preserving 1 GiB of sizing
headroom. Omission defaults to one --max-context worth of pages. The resolved pool is fixed at
startup and is not divided statically among request lanes.
Tool calls are parsed and returned to the client; NInfer does not execute tools.
The C++ headers are used by the in-tree applications and are not distributed as an installed SDK.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)

    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.

    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>

# Git and GitHub
- Only commit, amend, push, or create PRs when explicitly requested.
- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.
- Write a concise commit message that matches the repo style.
- Do not update git config, skip hooks, use interactive `-i`, force-push, or create empty commits unless explicitly requested.
- If a commit fails or hooks reject it, fix the issue and create a new commit; do not amend the failed commit.
- Before creating a PR, inspect status, diff, remote tracking, recent commits, and the diff from the base branch.
- Review all commits included in the PR, not just the latest commit.
- Use `gh` for GitHub tasks, including PRs, issues, checks, and releases; return the PR URL when done.

Issues live **exclusively on GitHub** (`gpillon/ignis`, via the `gh` CLI).

3: A high-throughput inference engine for **Qwen 3.8-27B** on a single **NVIDIA
4: RTX 5090** (SM120a), serving an **OpenAI-compatible HTTP API** from a Rust core
5: backed by a C++/CUDA kernel leaf.

7: **Status:** early development — **the engine now serves real completions on
8: the GPU.** With `IGNIS_ARTIFACT` set and the binary built with `--features
9: cuda`, `ignis-server` loads the model onto the device and drives the real
10: 64-layer program (device-resident, step-level C ABI — ADR 0009, verbatim-
11: vendored reference kernels — ADR 0010) for both streaming and non-streaming
12: chat completions, stopping on the model's own EOS token or `max_tokens`.
13: Without an artifact, or without `--features cuda`, it falls back to the
14: deterministic CPU-only mock (`MockCompute`, ADR 0006) for protocol and loop
15: work.

18: agreement), G2 GREEN (2026-09-09, TTFT ratios 0.878/0.851 on the 8K/32K

29: ## What it is
30: 
31: `ignis` is a deliberately specialized inference engine: one model family, one
32: GPU class. It is **not** a recreation of the reference stack (NInfer) — it is a
33: new architecture that borrows proven kernel work where it helps.
34: 
35: - **Performance-first.** Correctness (a self-check of *sane* output) is a
36:   non-negotiable floor; above it, performance is the #1 objective. The
37:   north-star is *"the best local coding engine"* — maximum throughput **and**
38:   agent parallelism that saturates the GPU in prefill *and* decode.
39: - **Rust core + C++/CUDA leaf.** Rust owns everything above the *step* —
40:   scheduling, KV accounting, serving; the forward pass and all GPU compute live
41:   in a static C++/CUDA library behind a flat, device-resident step-level C ABI
42:   (ADR 0009).

44: The engine is also its own dogfood target: good enough to run a developer's own
45: concurrent coding agent (a "1 main agent + N subagents" load).

1: # The vendored reference subtree
2: 
3: Everything under `kernel/vendor/` except this file is a **verbatim copy** of a
4: file from the reference engine (ninfer) at one pinned commit. Nothing here is
5: written or edited by hand. That is the whole point of ADR 0010: a port claim
6: must be diffable, so "we ported the reference's kernel" means *this exact file
7: is the reference's file*, and a script proves it.
8: 
9: - Policy: `docs/adr/0010-vendored-reference-kernels.md`
10: - Attribution: `kernel/NOTICE` (the subtree is Apache-2.0; `LICENSE` is
11:   vendored alongside the code)
12: - Spec: `.scratch/runtime/specs/01-device-resident-forward.md` (GitHub #36)
13: 
14: ## The manifest
15: 
16: `kernel/vendor/manifest.json` is the source of truth for what is vendored.
17: 
18: ```json
19: {
20:   "reference": { "repo": "…", "branch": "…", "commit": "…", "default_path": "…" },
21:   "vendor_root": "kernel/vendor",
22:   "files": [
23:     { "path": "src/core/arena.h", "sha256": "…" },
24:     { "path": "src/core/arena.cu", "sha256": "…",
25:       "patch": { "diff": "patches/src/core/arena.cu.diff", "sha256": "…", "reason": "…" } }
26:   ]
27: }
28: ```
29: 
30: - `reference.commit` is the **only** revision the hashes describe. Vendoring
31:   from any other checkout state is a hash mismatch, not a merge.
32: - `path` is shared by the reference and the leaf: `src/core/arena.h` in the
33:   reference is `kernel/vendor/src/core/arena.h` here. Vendored files keep the
34:   reference's namespaces and include paths (`#include "core/arena.h"`,
35:   `#include "ops/common/math.cuh"`), so a `diff` against the source is trivial
36:   and a reference update is a re-run of the script — never a re-port.
37: - `sha256` is the file's content hash **in the reference**. A vendored file
38:   must be byte-identical to it unless the entry records a `patch`.
39: - `.gitattributes` marks the subtree `-text` so git never rewrites the line
40:   endings the hashes describe.
41: 
42: ## The script
43: 
44: `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1` wraps the `vendor-ninfer` binary of
45: `crates/vendor`. The logic lives in a Rust crate rather than in the script so
46: that `cargo test` covers it (`docs/agents/testing.md`).
47: 
48: | Command | What it does |
49: |---|---|
50: | `verify` | Every listed file exists under `kernel/vendor/` and hashes to what the manifest expects. With a reference checkout present, also checks the reference still carries the pinned content. **This is the byte-identical check.** |
51: | `sync` | Copies every listed file from the reference into the leaf. Verifies the reference against the pinned hashes *first* and copies nothing on a mismatch, so a wrong checkout cannot half-overwrite the subtree. Files with a recorded patch are kept unless `--force-patched`. |
52: | `repin` | Recomputes the hashes from the checkout on disk. Used when moving to a new reference commit — set `reference.commit` in the same change. |
53: | `record-patch PATH --reason TEXT` | Writes the local edit out as a diff under `patches/` and records its patched hash. |
54: 
55: Options: `--reference PATH` (defaults to `reference.default_path`, or
56: `$IGNIS_NINFER_REFERENCE`), `--manifest PATH`. Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` a
57: verification finding, `2` a usage or I/O error. `verify` works without a
58: reference checkout, so it runs from a bare clone.
59: 
60: ```powershell
61: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 verify
62: ```
63: 
64: ## The patch policy
65: 
66: A vendored file may not be edited. When the leaf genuinely needs a local
67: change, it is **recorded**, never silently applied:
68: 
69: 1. edit the file under `kernel/vendor/`;
70: 2. `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 record-patch <path> --reason "<why>"` — this
71:    writes `patches/<path>.diff` and sets the entry's `patch.sha256` to the
72:    patched content's hash;
73: 3. commit the diff with the file.
74: 
75: From then on `verify` expects the *patched* hash locally and the *reference's*
76: hash upstream, so both an unrecorded edit and upstream drift are caught. `sync`
77: will not overwrite a patched file unless it is told to.
78: 
79: Anything that is not a verbatim vendored file — including a file we edit
80: beyond a recorded patch — is our own implementation and carries no provenance
81: claim (ADR 0010). The leaf's own code lives in `kernel/src/`,
82: `kernel/include/` and `kernel/tests/`, never here.

Why this fork
The upstream engine wasn't built with coding-agent workloads in mind. A tool like Qwen Code fires
bursts of near-identical subagent requests that share the same long system prompt and tool schemas
(often 98% identical) and diverge only in a short task-specific tail — but the engine had a single
global prefill lane with no concept of "these requests are mostly the same": every subagent redid
the full prefill from scratch, serialized one behind another, producing time-to-first-token ladders
of several seconds per subagent even though almost none of that work was actually new. A
long-running main conversation and a one-shot classifier call were also indistinguishable to the
scheduler, so the conversation the user was waiting on could get evicted and re-prefilled at the
worst possible moment. This fork exists to fix that: optimize the engine specifically for
coding-tool usage patterns.
What's added in this fork

Host-RAM KV cache tier (two-tier probation/protected eviction) that snapshots finished or
still-decoding GPU lanes so a sibling request can restore instead of re-prefilling
Prefix-reuse and admission logic so concurrent identical or shared-prefix requests (a subagent
burst sharing one long system+tools prompt) skip the redundant part of prefill entirely
Tagged request lanes (@main/@agents/@classifier, see below) so the scheduler knows which
lane is the long-lived conversation and protects it from eviction by short-lived traffic
DFlash2 speculative decoding made to actually run end-to-end on this tree (gather/selector
addressing bugs fixed, RAM-tier KV carry for the drafter, working presets)
Two silent KV-corruption bugs found and fixed (a rewrite-checkpoint restore and a hyperquant
exact-key side store, both serving one request with another's state)
Streaming/tool-call-parsing hardening, adaptive MTP verification-width calibration from measured
round cost

Measured effect: siblings that used to pay a full prefill (hundreds to thousands of ms) now restore
in tens to a few hundred ms, and a burst of subagents sharing a system+tools prefix reuses ~99% of
it instead of queueing behind each other's redundant prefill.

Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.8-27B each expose two registered weight profiles. The version-2 artifact
identity selects the profile without a separate runtime flag; Qwen3.8 uses target key
qwen3_8_27b while sharing the 27B execution package. The Qwen3.6 nvfp4 profile uses W4A4 Tensor
Core MMA for prefill and A16 NVFP4 kernels for decode. The Qwen3.8 nvfp4 profile preserves its
source's mixed allocation: NVFP4 MLP weights in Text layers 0–55 and row-scaled FP8 for the token
embedding, attention input/output projections, GDN Q/K/V/Z and output projections, output head, and
remaining MLP weights. All four 27B artifacts retain the same Text, Vision, MTP, prefix-reuse, CLI,
and serving routes.
Upstream lineage
NInfer is Neroued's project
(Neroued/ninfer); that repository remains the reference
implementation, and master here follows upstream/master directly. This workspace builds on
natpate/ninfer-windows, the native Windows port of
that engine — the port core below is inherited from it (the compatibility layer itself ported
from Don-Chad/ninfer-3090, without its RTX 3090
retargeting). The WebUI and context-reporting items live on this fork's feat/windows-port
lineage — natpate's dev branch has already absorbed them, and PR #2
delivers them to its master.
Windows-port lineage:

Native Windows 11 x64 build and run — CMake with Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC), with
vcpkg resolving FFmpeg, libcurl, and zlib via the
vcpkg.json manifest; the CUDA runtime is statically linked, so the CUDA Toolkit is only
needed at build time.
Windows porting of the runtime — memory-mapped artifact reading with unbuffered
overlapped I/O (the Windows counterpart of POSIX O_DIRECT/pread, with the same 4096-byte
alignment contract), portable console logging and load progress, and portable media
acquisition for image and video input.
MSVC/TMA kernel compatibility — fixes that let the upstream Blackwell kernels compile
under MSVC: device-pointer NVFP4 TMA descriptors, the pair-row SwiGLU TMA epilogue, and
MSVC move-construction details in the target runtime.
Stock llama.cpp WebUI — the HTTP server additionally accepts the stock llama.cpp WebUI's
API dialect, and ninfer-serve can serve the unmodified WebUI in-process: --webui
downloads the latest build from the
ggml-org/llama-ui bucket on first start, or
--webui-dir DIR serves an existing local copy.
Context window reporting — ninfer-serve advertises the served context ceiling in the
OpenAI dialect: the objects returned by /v1/models and /v1/models/{id} carry
meta.n_ctx = the --max-context value in force.
Portable Windows release — a self-contained zip containing the executables and all
runtime DLLs; see Prebuilt Windows release.

What this fork adds on top (one squashed commit per feature branch, per
About this fork):

feat/qwen3.8-nvfp4full — the Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 full-precision-requant artifact:
unified activation scale space, conversion tooling, model card, and the published gpqa
comparison.
feat/hyperquant — the hq-e8-2b KV cache: E8-lattice + Rice entropy coding at
2.25 bits/scalar (3.7× smaller payload than INT8 at 262k context), prompt attention over
one-shot decoded rotated bf16 scratch, an 8-lane cooperative k=0 Rice decoder with a
parallel unary packer, and a tensor-core tile-source decode kernel (the hq route is a
KV-source policy of the bf16 TC kernel). After the residual-window + dither work below,
hq decode matches or beats same-session INT8 at the measured cells (tg128 80.6 vs 71.7,
pp32k+tg64 62.2 vs 58.1 tok/s).
feat/1m-context — the 1M-context track: engine envelope raised to 1,048,576 keys on
the U8 cache (banded rotated scratch, 1M + --kv-capacity auto resolves the full pool with
~3.3 GiB free), YaRN rope scaling (--rope-scaling yarn:F[,t=][,bf=][,bs=], q-side
temperature, FP64 angle reduction), the bf16/int8 linear envelope raised to 524,288 keys,
and the WI-8 quality fix — a BF16 sink+recent residual window (S=32/W=512 exact side rows
with per-slot ring validity) plus half-cell subtractive dither, which fixed the >262k hq
garble: greedy needle retrieval is exact at 32k/304k/390k/592k true tokens (592k runs
yarn:4 at 916–922 prefill / 15.2 decode tok/s; MTP3 at 390k commits 62.9 tok/s). Beyond
~592k the 1M cell still garbles (depth-independent; dense-YaRN-at-1M is the leading
suspect — see HANDOFF).

Everything else — the Linux build path, the RTX 5090 (sm_120a) target, the CUDA 13.1
requirement, and the NVFP4/W4A4 Blackwell execution paths — is unchanged from upstream.

Requirements
NInfer currently requires:

64-bit Linux or Windows 11 x64;
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120a);
NVIDIA driver support for CUDA 13.1 and the CUDA Toolkit 13.1 or newer;
CMake 3.28 or newer and a C++20-capable host compiler (GCC or Clang on Linux, MSVC from
Visual Studio 2022 on Windows);
FFmpeg development libraries: libavformat >= 60, libavcodec >= 60,
libavutil >= 58, and libswscale >= 7;
libcurl >= 7.85;
pkg-config on Linux, or vcpkg on Windows (the
repository pins the dependency baseline in vcpkg.json);
Ninja, when using the commands below.

The build rejects CUDA architectures other than 120a. On Linux, NInfer is run from its
source build tree; on Windows, the prebuilt portable release
provides the same binaries without a toolchain.
Prebuilt Windows release
Windows users who would rather not build can use the portable release instead of the build
steps below. The zip is self-contained — executables, all runtime DLLs (FFmpeg,
libcurl, zlib, and the VC++ runtime; the CUDA runtime is statically linked), launcher scripts,
a models\ folder, a README.txt, and SHA256SUMS:

Download the latest ninfer-windows-<version>-win64-cuda131.zip from
GitHub Releases. Verify files against
SHA256SUMS, e.g. Get-FileHash ninfer-serve.exe -Algorithm SHA256.
Extract it anywhere — the launcher scripts use relative paths and work from any location.
Download a model into models\ as in Download a model.
Run the matching launcher, e.g. .\qwen3_8_27b.bat. This starts ninfer-serve on
http://127.0.0.1:8080 (API at /v1) and serves the WebUI at the root URL; --webui
downloads the WebUI on first start, so the first run needs an internet connection (later
runs reuse the local copy).
Or run .\ninfer-serve.exe models\<model>.ninfer [flags] directly — the options are
identical to a source build (see Run the HTTP server).

The launchers default to a 150,000-token context (--max-context / --default-max-tokens) to
leave VRAM headroom for the Windows desktop. On the 32 GB RTX 5090, the smaller models
(qwen3_6_27b, qwen3_6_27b_nvfp4, and qwen3_8_27b) can be safely raised to 200,000 when
VRAM is completely free at startup; the two larger models (qwen3_8_27b_nvfp4 and
qwen3_6_35b_a3b) do not fit at 200,000 and should stay at 150,000. Hardware requirements are
unchanged: Windows 11 x64, RTX 5090, and an NVIDIA driver supporting CUDA 13.1.
Build

git clone https://github.com/cometkim/ninfer.git
cd ninfer

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel

build/apps/ninfer

Tests, benchmarks, and maintainer tools are excluded from the default build.
Windows
The fork's build entry point is a pair of plain-PowerShell Ninja wrappers — no developer
prompt needed. configure-ninja.ps1 (run once per build directory) imports the MSVC
(vcvars64) environment itself, resolves cmake/ninja from PATH with VS-bundled and
winget fallbacks, points the vcpkg toolchain at VCPKG_ROOT (falling back to this
machine's local checkout) and nvcc at CUDA_PATH, and enables tests and benchmarks by
default (-NoTests / -NoBenchmarks exclude them). build-ninja.ps1 builds everything
or one target:
git clone https://github.com/cometkim/ninfer.git
cd ninfer

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File configure-ninja.ps1
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File build-ninja.ps1
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File build-ninja.ps1 -Target ninfer_bench
The default configuration builds:

For
Eviction priority




@main

protected — ranked last among eviction candidates, so short-lived traffic never forces it to re-prefill


@agents

  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{

    "max_tokens": 256
  }'

# separate so its churn is visible on its own in the throughput log.

  }'

mid-decode, and the main conversation's lane is never chosen as the eviction victim — the subagents
recycle each other's lanes first. Subagents sharing a system+tools prefix restore most of it from
the host-RAM cache instead of re-prefilling, so time-to-first-token drops from full-prefill latency
(hundreds of ms to multiple seconds, depending on prompt length) to the cost of re-hashing and
copying a cached prefix (tens to a couple hundred ms). Untagged requests keep working exactly as

Capabilities
All three registered model IDs support:

text generation with thinking and non-thinking prompt modes;
image, multi-image, video, and mixed multimodal messages;
chunked prefill and CUDA Graph decode;
startup-bounded small-scale concurrent serving with true batched decode;
fixed or signal-adaptive MTP speculative decoding with draft windows from one to eight on 27B
targets and one to five on 35B-A3B;
BF16 and INT8 group-64 KV cache;
model- and thinking-mode-aware official sampling defaults, with explicit greedy, temperature,
top-k, top-p, min-p, and presence/frequency-penalty overrides;
compatible-prefix reuse;
OpenAI Responses Core, OpenAI Chat Completions, and Anthropic Messages, including streaming and
usage accounting;
prompt-rendered function tools and parsed tool calls.

The 35B-A3B target additionally supports text-only DFlash speculative decoding with draft windows
from one to fifteen.
Current limits

Only the five (model_id, weights_id) artifact identities listed above are accepted product
identities.
Execution is specialized for one RTX 5090 and one CUDA device.
One Engine owns one resident model and supports a startup-fixed capacity of 1–8 active requests.
Decode-ready requests are compacted at round boundaries and executed in one batched model
traversal.
NInfer does not provide large-scale or preemptive continuous batching, priority/QoS scheduling,
multi-GPU execution, CPU/GPU offload, or distributed serving.
--max-context is the logical ceiling of each sequence and is configurable up to the registered
models' per-dtype context envelope: 524,288 tokens with bf16/int8 KV and 1,048,576
with hq-e8-2b (YaRN --rope-scaling yarn:F past the checkpoint's trained 262,144
positions). --kv-capacity N explicitly sizes the shared Main Text KV
pool for all active and retained sequences, while --kv-capacity auto selects the largest usable
capacity from the memory remaining after weights are loaded while preserving 1 GiB of sizing
headroom. Omission defaults to one --max-context worth of pages. The resolved pool is fixed at
startup and is not divided statically among request lanes.
Tool calls are parsed and returned to the client; NInfer does not execute tools.
The C++ headers are used by the in-tree applications and are not distributed as an installed SDK.

## Agent skills

### Issue tracker

Issues live **exclusively on GitHub** (`gpillon/ignis`, via the `gh` CLI).
GitHub is the single source of truth for issue tracking: status, blocking
relationships, labels, and closure. Each GitHub issue body is short
(1-3 lines of context) and links to the implementation spec.

Implementation specs (acceptance criteria, seam description, ADR references)
live under `.scratch/<feature>/specs/` in this repo. These are **specs, not
issues** — they do not track status or blocking (that is GitHub's job).
`.scratch/` is also used for temporary artifacts, experiments, and workflow
output, but **never for issue tracking**.

See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` for the full convention.

### Triage labels

The five canonical triage roles, mapped 1:1 to same-name labels
(`needs-triage`, `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, `wontfix`).
See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

Single-context — root `CONTEXT.md` for the glossary, `docs/adr/` for ADRs.
See `docs/agents/domain.md`.

### Findings

When recording or consulting durable findings from discovery, research, or
experiments, start from `docs/findings/README.md`.

### Testing

Every code change ships with a test, and the task is not complete until
`cargo test` passes workspace-wide. Before launching **anything** on the GPU
(the profile, a bench run, a gate leg, one `--ignored` test), always check
that no other test, bench or agent session is already using the card — in
any worktree. The 5090 fits one run at a time and the loser dies with no
diagnostic. See `docs/agents/testing.md`.

### Make

`make help` lists the targets; `make config` prints the exact server command
a run will use. An agent runs the server as a daemon — `make start`, then
`make stop` — since `run`, `dev`, `dev-ui` and `watch` hold the terminal
until Ctrl+C. `run` and `start` only ever launch the last build: a stale
binary fails naming the changed files, and `make build` is the fix.
`make gpu-status` is the one-command check before GPU work. Why it is
shaped this way: ADR 0027.

### Worktrees

All git worktrees for this repo live under `../.inference-qwen-worktrees/`
(sibling of the repo root), one subdirectory per issue/feature. Do not create
worktrees anywhere else (e.g. no separate `.inference-claude-worktrees/`) —
one shared location for every agent.

1: # ignis
2: 
3: A high-throughput inference engine for **Qwen 3.8-27B** on a single **NVIDIA
4: RTX 5090** (SM120a), serving an **OpenAI-compatible HTTP API** from a Rust core
5: backed by a C++/CUDA kernel leaf.
6: 
7: **Status:** early development — **the engine now serves real completions on
8: the GPU.** With `IGNIS_ARTIFACT` set and the binary built with `--features
9: cuda`, `ignis-server` loads the model onto the device and drives the real
10: 64-layer program (device-resident, step-level C ABI — ADR 0009, verbatim-
11: vendored reference kernels — ADR 0010) for both streaming and non-streaming
12: chat completions, stopping on the model's own EOS token or `max_tokens`.
13: Without an artifact, or without `--features cuda`, it falls back to the
14: deterministic CPU-only mock (`MockCompute`, ADR 0006) for protocol and loop
15: work.
16: 
17: **Gate history:** G1 GREEN (2026-09-07, 97.1% teacher-forced canary
18: agreement), G2 GREEN (2026-09-09, TTFT ratios 0.878/0.851 on the 8K/32K
19: cells), G3 closed 2026-09-10 with one open gap (#110, the ITL p95 cell).
20: **Next milestone: the G4 gate run** (master #65, the reference feature
21: floor) — hq-e8-2b KV as a load option, snapshot/restore + KV-RAM host tier,
22: device prefix reuse, unified eviction, tagged lanes; verdict is the 99%
23: performance gate (ADR 0007) on the recorded "1 main + N subagents" load.
24: The full phase/gate plan is `.scratch/ROADMAP.md`; the review that reset it
25: is `.scratch/REVIEW-2026-09-05.md`.
26: 
27: ---
28: 
29: ## What it is
30: 
31: `ignis` is a deliberately specialized inference engine: one model family, one
32: GPU class. It is **not** a recreation of the reference stack (NInfer) — it is a
33: new architecture that borrows proven kernel work where it helps.
34: 
35: - **Performance-first.** Correctness (a self-check of *sane* output) is a
36:   non-negotiable floor; above it, performance is the #1 objective. The
37:   north-star is *"the best local coding engine"* — maximum throughput **and**
38:   agent parallelism that saturates the GPU in prefill *and* decode.
39: - **Rust core + C++/CUDA leaf.** Rust owns everything above the *step* —
40:   scheduling, KV accounting, serving; the forward pass and all GPU compute live
41:   in a static C++/CUDA library behind a flat, device-resident step-level C ABI
42:   (ADR 0009).
43: 
44: The engine is also its own dogfood target: good enough to run a developer's own
45: concurrent coding agent (a "1 main agent + N subagents" load).
46: 
47: ## Architecture
48: 
49: Two layers, plus the artifact that carries the weights and the frontend
50: objects. Items marked *(planned)* are the G1–G4 build-out, not shipped code:
51: 
52: ```
53: HTTP (OpenAI-compatible: /v1/models, /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses)
54:   │
55: Rust core (crates/core)
56:   ├── Scheduler: prefill + N=8 decode lanes (host-tier overflow)
57:   │              + full admission state machine (protection / backfill class /
58:   │              temporal credit / frontier distance)
59:   ├── Paged KV page accounting + block tables (device pages reported by the leaf)
60:   ├── KV-RAM host tier (probation / protected eviction) + prefix reuse *(in progress: G4)*
61:   ├── Artifact loader (.ninfer reader + binder + materializer + device views)
62:   ├── Telemetry (JSONL interval lines; request lifecycle as structured logs)
63:   └── crates/runtime: safe wrapper over the step ABI *(shipped: G1)*
64:         │
65: Step-level C ABI (device-resident, opaque handles — ADR 0009)
66:   model load · sequence alloc/release/snapshot · prefill(span, pos)
67:   · decode round(batch) · sampling params · stats
68:         │
69: Kernel leaf (kernel/, C++/CUDA static lib — CMake + nvcc, SM120a)
70:   ├── program: device arena, streams, the 64-layer op sequence,
71:   │            sequence state (KV pages, fp32 GDN slots, conv taps)
72:   └── vendored ops (verbatim from the reference, ADR 0010)
73:       ├── NVFP4 / BF16 / W8G32 linear (GEMV, small-T; W4A4 + TMA since G2)
74:       ├── GQA attention (bf16 + hq-e8-2b paged decode + prefill; i8 unused)
75:       ├── GDN family (causal conv1d + SiLU, gating, recurrence, chunked since G2)
76:       ├── norms / embedding / sampling
77:       └── per-width decode CUDA graphs *(shipped: G3, widths 1..8)*
78: ```

12: # GitHub #135. The GPU profile's f64 layer oracles are CPU-bound on scalar
13: # `f64` with per-element NVFP4 / W8 dequantization, and at the default
14: # `opt-level = 0` they dominated the serialized `--ignored` stage. The real
15: # two-layer oracle (`layer_reference_real`) took 123.94 s there; optimizing

17: # it runs in ~3.9 s. The oracle lives in a library crate, so `[profile.test]`
18: # alone would not reach it -- `cargo test` builds dependencies with `dev`,
19: # and only the test targets themselves with `test`.

21: # Rust applies no fast-math, so every `f64` result -- and therefore every
22: # measured tolerance in the profile -- is bit-identical to the unoptimized
23: # build. `debug-assertions` (and the overflow checks that follow them) stay
24: # on in both profiles: this buys speed, never fewer checks.

1: # The vendored reference subtree
2: 
3: Everything under `kernel/vendor/` except this file is a **verbatim copy** of a
4: file from the reference engine (ninfer) at one pinned commit. Nothing here is
5: written or edited by hand. That is the whole point of ADR 0010: a port claim
6: must be diffable, so "we ported the reference's kernel" means *this exact file
7: is the reference's file*, and a script proves it.
8: 
9: - Policy: `docs/adr/0010-vendored-reference-kernels.md`
10: - Attribution: `kernel/NOTICE` (the subtree is Apache-2.0; `LICENSE` is
11:   vendored alongside the code)
12: - Spec: `.scratch/runtime/specs/01-device-resident-forward.md` (GitHub #36)
13: 
14: ## The manifest
15: 
16: `kernel/vendor/manifest.json` is the source of truth for what is vendored.
17: 
18: ```json
19: {
20:   "reference": { "repo": "…", "branch": "…", "commit": "…", "default_path": "…" },
21:   "vendor_root": "kernel/vendor",
22:   "files": [
23:     { "path": "src/core/arena.h", "sha256": "…" },
24:     { "path": "src/core/arena.cu", "sha256": "…",
25:       "patch": { "diff": "patches/src/core/arena.cu.diff", "sha256": "…", "reason": "…" } }
26:   ]
27: }
28: ```
29: 
30: - `reference.commit` is the **only** revision the hashes describe. Vendoring
31:   from any other checkout state is a hash mismatch, not a merge.
32: - `path` is shared by the reference and the leaf: `src/core/arena.h` in the
33:   reference is `kernel/vendor/src/core/arena.h` here. Vendored files keep the
34:   reference's namespaces and include paths (`#include "core/arena.h"`,
35:   `#include "ops/common/math.cuh"`), so a `diff` against the source is trivial
36:   and a reference update is a re-run of the script — never a re-port.
37: - `sha256` is the file's content hash **in the reference**. A vendored file
38:   must be byte-identical to it unless the entry records a `patch`.
39: - `.gitattributes` marks the subtree `-text` so git never rewrites the line
40:   endings the hashes describe.
41: 
42: ## The script
43: 
44: `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1` wraps the `vendor-ninfer` binary of
45: `crates/vendor`. The logic lives in a Rust crate rather than in the script so
46: that `cargo test` covers it (`docs/agents/testing.md`).
47: 
48: | Command | What it does |
49: |---|---|
50: | `verify` | Every listed file exists under `kernel/vendor/` and hashes to what the manifest expects. With a reference checkout present, also checks the reference still carries the pinned content. **This is the byte-identical check.** |
51: | `sync` | Copies every listed file from the reference into the leaf. Verifies the reference against the pinned hashes *first* and copies nothing on a mismatch, so a wrong checkout cannot half-overwrite the subtree. Files with a recorded patch are kept unless `--force-patched`. |
52: | `repin` | Recomputes the hashes from the checkout on disk. Used when moving to a new reference commit — set `reference.commit` in the same change. |
53: | `record-patch PATH --reason TEXT` | Writes the local edit out as a diff under `patches/` and records its patched hash. |
54: 
55: Options: `--reference PATH` (defaults to `reference.default_path`, or
56: `$IGNIS_NINFER_REFERENCE`), `--manifest PATH`. Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` a
57: verification finding, `2` a usage or I/O error. `verify` works without a
58: reference checkout, so it runs from a bare clone.
59: 
60: ```powershell
61: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 verify
62: ```
63: 
64: ## The patch policy
65: 
66: A vendored file may not be edited. When the leaf genuinely needs a local
67: change, it is **recorded**, never silently applied:
68: 
69: 1. edit the file under `kernel/vendor/`;
70: 2. `scripts/vendor-ninfer.ps1 record-patch <path> --reason "<why>"` — this
71:    writes `patches/<path>.diff` and sets the entry's `patch.sha256` to the
72:    patched content's hash;
73: 3. commit the diff with the file.
74: 
75: From then on `verify` expects the *patched* hash locally and the *reference's*
76: hash upstream, so both an unrecorded edit and upstream drift are caught. `sync`
77: will not overwrite a patched file unless it is told to.
78: 
79: Anything that is not a verbatim vendored file — including a file we edit
80: beyond a recorded patch — is our own implementation and carries no provenance
81: claim (ADR 0010). The leaf's own code lives in `kernel/src/`,
82: `kernel/include/` and `kernel/tests/`, never here.
83:
